section.title: Jeremiah Threatened with Death
section.sectionRationale: This chapter narrates in full the mortal danger Jeremiah's preaching provoked: seized by priests and prophets and threatened with death for prophesying the temple's destruction, he is spared only when officials and elders recall Micah's precedent, while another prophet, Uriah, who spoke the identical word, is hunted down and executed.
section.thesis: Jeremiah's temple sermon, that even God's own house can fall like Shiloh if the people will not turn, nearly costs him his life, and only Micah's remembered precedent and Ahikam's protection save him, while Uriah's fate for the same true word shows just how real the danger was.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: the command to speak and the mob's seizure of the prophet, Jeremiah's own defense before the officials and their verdict, and the precedent of Micah set against the execution of Uriah for the identical word.

verses.text: At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah, this word came from the LORD:

“This is what the LORD says: Stand in the courtyard of the house of the LORD and speak all the words I have commanded you to speak to all the cities of Judah who come to worship there. Do not omit a word.
Perhaps they will listen and turn, each from his evil way of life, so that I may {{nacham|relent}} of the disaster I am planning to bring upon them because of the evil of their deeds.
And you are to tell them that this is what the LORD says: ‘If you do not listen to Me and walk in My law, which I have set before you,
and if you do not listen to the words of My servants the prophets, whom I have sent you again and again even though you did not listen,
then I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city an object of cursing among all the nations of the earth.’”
Now the priests and prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the LORD,
and as soon as he had finished telling all the people everything the LORD had commanded him to say, the priests and prophets and all the people seized him, shouting, “You must surely die!

How dare you prophesy in the name of the LORD that this house will become like Shiloh and this city will be desolate and deserted!” 
And all the people assembled against Jeremiah in the house of the LORD.
When the officials of Judah heard these things, they went up from the king's palace to the house of the LORD and sat there at the entrance of the New Gate.
Then the priests and prophets said to the officials and all the people, “This man is worthy of death, for he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears!”
But Jeremiah said to all the officials and all the people, “The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that you have heard.
So now, correct your ways and deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, so that He might relent of the disaster He has pronounced against you.
As for me, here I am in your hands; do to me what you think is good and right.

But know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring {{daminnaqi|innocent blood}} upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its residents; for truly the LORD has sent me to speak all these words in your hearing.”
Then the officials and all the people told the priests and prophets, “This man is not worthy of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God!”

units.label: Micah's precedent, Uriah's fate
units.note: one spared, one killed for the same word

verses.text: Some of the elders of the land stood up and said to the whole assembly of the people,

“Micah the Moreshite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah and told all the people of Judah that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: 
‘Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, 
and the temple mount a wooded ridge.’

Did Hezekiah king of Judah or anyone else in Judah put him to death? Did Hezekiah not fear the LORD and seek His favor, and did not the LORD relent of the disaster He had pronounced against them? But we are about to bring great harm on ourselves!”
Now there was another man prophesying in the name of the LORD, Uriah son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied against this city and against this land the same things that Jeremiah did.
King Jehoiakim and all his mighty men and officials heard his words, and the king sought to put him to death. But when Uriah found out about it, he fled in fear and went to Egypt.
Then King Jehoiakim sent men to Egypt: Elnathan son of Achbor along with some other men.
They brought Uriah out of Egypt and took him to King Jehoiakim, who had him put to the sword and his body thrown into the burial place of the common people.
Nevertheless, Ahikam son of Shaphan supported Jeremiah, so he was not handed over to the people to be put to death.

nacham.gloss: To relent, to change course in response to genuine turning. God's warning of disaster is not a fixed decree independent of human response; He says plainly that if the people turn, He will nacham, relent, exactly the pattern He honored for Hezekiah and Judah in Micah's day, verse 19.

daminnaqi.gloss: Innocent blood, a phrase carrying serious legal and covenantal weight in Israel, since shedding it brought guilt on the whole community, not just the guilty individual. Jeremiah warns that killing him for speaking a true word from the LORD would bring exactly this weight of guilt on the entire city.

basic.context: God commands Jeremiah to stand in the temple courtyard and preach the same hard warning as the temple sermon, that the house of the LORD itself could become a ruin like Shiloh if the people will not turn. The priests and prophets who hear it seize Jeremiah and demand his death for daring to say such a thing about God's own house, but the elders remember that King Hezekiah spared the prophet Micah for an almost identical warning, and Jeremiah is released, while another prophet, Uriah, who spoke the same true word, is later hunted down in Egypt and executed.
basic.hermeneutics: This is straightforward historical narrative, recounting a real trial with a real, named precedent cited from Israel's own history, Micah's prophecy roughly a century earlier. The sobering detail readers must not soften is that the very same message that saved Jeremiah's life, because of Hezekiah's godly example, ended Uriah's life under a different, ungodly king, showing that faithfulness to God's word does not guarantee safety, only that God is faithful regardless of the outcome.
basic.originalLanguages: The heart of Jeremiah's appeal is that God will nacham, relent, of disaster if the people turn, precisely the pattern Israel's own history proved true under Hezekiah. And Jeremiah's warning to his accusers is that killing him would bring dam naqi, innocent blood, upon the whole city, a phrase carrying real covenantal weight, since unaddressed innocent blood defiled the entire community, not only the individual killer.
basic.typology: Jeremiah's trial before priests, prophets, and officials, on the charge of threatening the temple, directly anticipates Jesus' own trial before the Sanhedrin, where the same accusation, threatening to destroy the temple, is brought against Him, Matthew 26:61. Uriah's execution for speaking God's true word previews the cost the greater Prophet, Christ, would ultimately pay for the very same faithfulness.
basic.christ: The charge brought against Jeremiah, that he prophesied the temple's destruction, is the identical charge later brought against Jesus at His trial, Matthew 26:61, and like Jeremiah, Jesus stood before hostile religious authorities who wanted Him dead for speaking a true and unwelcome word. Where Jeremiah was spared through Ahikam's protection and Micah's precedent, Jesus was not spared, willingly drinking the cup others were rescued from, so that His death, unlike Uriah's, would accomplish the world's redemption rather than merely silence an inconvenient voice.
basic.god: God is patient and genuinely responsive to repentance, still holding out the possibility that He will relent even after pronouncing disaster, and He remains faithful to His true messengers even when the outcome differs wildly from one to another, sparing Jeremiah while allowing Uriah's death. His justice held Judah accountable for shedding innocent blood, a standard that exposes just how seriously God regards the mistreatment of those who speak His word.
basic.crossReferences: Micah 3:12 records the actual prophecy the elders cite as precedent, confirming its historical accuracy within Scripture itself. Matthew 26:61 shows the identical charge, threatening the temple, brought against Jesus at His own trial. Acts 7:52 recalls a long pattern of Israel killing the prophets who spoke God's truth, of which Uriah is a stark example. 1 Kings 19:10 shows Elijah lamenting this same pattern of prophets being killed for faithful ministry.
basic.oneStory: Jeremiah's near escape and Uriah's execution for the identical faithful word show how costly it has always been to carry God's true message into a hostile world. That pattern of persecuted truth-telling reaches its climax in Christ, who faced the same charge Jeremiah faced and, unlike Jeremiah, was not spared, so that His death would become the means of life for everyone who receives His word.

context.literary:
Chapter 26 opens a new block of the book, and its first line, 'At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim,' Jeremiah 26:1, pushes the clock back to about 609 BC, well before the Zedekiah-era chapters around it. The editor has placed it here because it explains how a prophet of doom survived long enough to write a book of hope. The account is a courtroom drama in three movements. In verses 1 to 9 the word is spoken and the crowd seizes the speaker. In verses 10 to 19 the case moves from a mob to a hearing, with the accusers speaking in verse 11, the defendant in verses 12 to 15, and the verdict and the elders' appeal to precedent in verses 16 to 19. Verses 20 to 24 then add a counter-case that threatens to undo the happy ending.

The passage is built on echoes. The command 'Perhaps they will listen,' verse 3, is answered by the crowd that does not, and by the officials who, strikingly, do. The phrase 'worthy of death' is spoken by the priests and prophets in verse 11 and reversed by the officials in verse 16, in almost the same words. The elders in verse 19 end with a warning that is really a sermon, 'we are about to bring great harm on ourselves.' Notice also that Jeremiah's defence contains no defence of himself. He offers no argument for his own safety; he repeats the message, urges repentance a second time in verse 13, and hands himself over in verse 14.

The story of Uriah in verses 20 to 23 is the odd piece, and it is placed last on purpose. A tidy ending would stop at verse 19. By closing with a prophet who said the same things and was executed, the narrator refuses to let the reader conclude that obedience always ends well. Verse 24 then turns on a single word, 'Nevertheless,' and credits Jeremiah's survival to one named protector rather than to the strength of his case.
context.historical:
The scene is set in Jehoiakim's accession year, after Pharaoh Neco had removed Jehoahaz and installed Eliakim under the new name Jehoiakim, 2 Kings 23:34. Josiah's reform, which had centred worship on the temple, had ended in his death at Megiddo, and the nation was now a vassal of Egypt. Many in Jerusalem drew a confident conclusion: the temple had kept the city safe through Sennacherib's siege in Hezekiah's day, and it would do so again. Jeremiah's temple sermon, recorded at greater length in Jeremiah 7:1 to 15, attacked exactly that confidence. 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD,' he mimics in Jeremiah 7:4, and he sends them to look at Shiloh, Jeremiah 7:12, the shrine where the ark had once rested and which God had abandoned, Psalm 78:60.

The charge was serious in Israel's law. Deuteronomy 18:20 says a prophet who speaks in God's name what God has not commanded 'must be put to death,' and the priests and prophets in verse 11 are applying that law to what they honestly believe is a false prophecy. They are not simple villains; they are guardians of a sacred place who hear an attack on it as blasphemy.

The officials who come up from the palace to sit at the entrance of the New Gate are the court of first resort, and their instinct is legal rather than religious. The elders cite Micah 3:12 from about a century earlier, spoken in Hezekiah's time, Micah 1:1. The cast of verses 20 to 24 matters too. Elnathan son of Achbor, who is sent to drag Uriah back from Egypt, comes from a family of Josiah's officials, 2 Kings 22:12, and Jeremiah 36:25 later shows him pleading with the king not to burn the scroll. Ahikam son of Shaphan belongs to the scribal family that had carried Josiah's book to the king, and the same family keeps appearing at Jeremiah's side, Jeremiah 29:3, Jeremiah 36:10 and 2 Kings 25:22.
context.canonical:
The chapter draws two Old Testament texts into one trial. Micah 3:12, quoted by the elders, is cited here as case law, and it is introduced with the prophet's name, town and date. Its context in Micah 3:9 to 12 shows why it fits so well: rulers who judge for a bribe, priests who teach for a price, and prophets who lean on the LORD and say 'No disaster can come upon us.' The elders also remember what Micah's book does not report, that Hezekiah feared the LORD and the disaster was withheld. That memory is the principle stated in Jeremiah 18:7 to 10, which says announcements of judgment are open to repentance.

The Shiloh warning links Jeremiah 7, Jeremiah 26 and Psalm 78:60, and it also reaches back to 1 Samuel 4, where the ark did not protect an Israel that treated it as a charm.

Jeremiah's fate becomes the template for the prophets' fate in the rest of Scripture. Jesus laments that Jerusalem 'kills the prophets and stones those sent to her,' Luke 13:34, and says it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem, Luke 13:33. Stephen asks which prophet the fathers did not persecute, Acts 7:52. In Matthew 23:35 the blood of the righteous is reckoned from Abel to Zechariah, and the warning that Jeremiah gives, that innocent blood would fall on the city, Jeremiah 26:15, is the same language the crowd uses of itself at the cross, Matthew 27:25. At Jesus' trial the charge that He would destroy the temple, Matthew 26:61 and John 2:19, is the same accusation Jeremiah faced, though Jesus was speaking of the temple of His body.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The book's compilers placed this chapter to answer a question every reader of Jeremiah must ask: why did anyone keep listening to a man whom the establishment wanted dead? The chapter shows the first hearers that Jeremiah was no traitor and no madman. He spoke what God commanded, 'Do not omit a word,' Jeremiah 26:2, and he did so in the most public place, to the most hostile audience, at the cost of his life. It also tells them, quietly, what the real question is. The point of the sermon is not whether the temple will fall but whether people will 'correct your ways and deeds,' verse 13.

The chapter also asks the reader to take sides. Will we be with the priests and prophets who seize the messenger, with the officials who listen, or with Jehoiakim who hunts a man down? The elders' memory of Micah is meant to teach that listening is possible, that the people of God have done it before, and that it spares everyone. Finally, the closing story of Uriah is there to stop the reader reading the book as a formula. The same word can be heard and spared, or heard and killed. Jeremiah's survival rests on God's providence working through a family of officials, not on the quality of his argument.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a trial, a verdict and an execution. It does not command anyone to cite precedent, to resist a mob or to flee to Egypt. What it reports is what happened, and the narrator is careful not to praise Uriah or blame him for running. Reading verse 21 as a rule that prophets should flee, or verse 14 as a rule that prophets should surrender, would turn two different responses of two different men into laws.

What does carry forward is the pattern of faithfulness under threat. The messenger says everything he was told, including the unwelcome part, and then leaves the outcome to God. The believer today is not promised Jeremiah's rescue and is not shielded from Uriah's end. The New Testament says plainly that some of the faithful were killed by the sword, Hebrews 11:37, and that disciples should expect hostility, Luke 6:22 to 23. The text also gives a modest application for communities: the wisdom of earlier generations, here Micah and Hezekiah, may be the very thing that keeps a congregation from a hasty and harmful judgment on a hard word.

debates.question: Does God really 'relent,' and if so, how does that fit with a God who does not change His mind?

views.label: Announcements of judgment are conditional by nature
views.case: Jeremiah 18:7 to 10 sets out the rule: a threat of disaster is withdrawn if the nation turns, and a promise of blessing is withdrawn if the nation turns to evil. On this view the prophet's warning in 26:3 and 26:13 is itself an invitation, the God who relents is acting consistently with His unchanging character, and Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 speak of God's not being fickle or deceitful, not of His being deaf to repentance.

views.label: Relenting is human-sounding language for God's real responsiveness
views.case: Others take the verb as an anthropomorphism that describes from our side what looks like a change, while God's eternal purpose, including the means of repentance by which He accomplishes it, never alters. Hezekiah's fear of the LORD in verse 19 is then a means God ordains to the outcome He decreed.

views.label: God genuinely enters a real exchange with His people
views.case: A third view holds that the text means what it says: God's plans are open to His creatures' responses, and He truly chooses a different course because they have turned. Defenders point to the open 'perhaps' of 26:3. Critics reply that Jeremiah 26:3 expresses the prophet's hope as to the people's response, not uncertainty in God.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on the practical point that Jeremiah presses in verse 13: the right response to a threat from God is to turn, and that response is never wasted.

debates.question: Is this chapter the same event as the temple sermon in Jeremiah 7?

views.label: Chapter 26 is a narrative frame around chapter 7
views.case: Both speak of Shiloh and the temple, and chapter 26 summarises the message while chapter 7 gives the sermon's body. Chapter 7 gives the content and chapter 26 the aftermath, with the dating 'beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim' placing both in 609 to 608 BC.

views.label: Two related occasions
views.case: Others note that chapter 7 sets Jeremiah at the gate of the house of the LORD, while chapter 26 sets him in the courtyard, and that chapter 26 reports the warning in a shorter form. They suggest Jeremiah preached the same warning more than once, and that chapter 26 reports a later, shorter form.

debates.bearing: The difference does not change the message. Either way the book is telling us that the temple sermon cost Jeremiah his freedom, and that the cost is part of the word.

study.originalLanguages:
Several Hebrew features sharpen the story. The crowd shouts 'You must surely die!' in verse 8, which is the same doubled form, 'dying you will die,' that God used in Genesis 2:17. The people claim the right to carry out the sentence the law reserves for a false prophet, Deuteronomy 18:20, and the officials in verse 11 are asked to give a 'judgment of death,' literally the phrase behind 'worthy of death.' The elders' verdict in verse 16 answers it in kind.

The command 'Do not omit a word' in verse 2 uses a verb meaning to take away or diminish. It is the same family of words as the ban on subtracting from the law in Deuteronomy 4:2, which makes the prophet's task parallel to the lawgiver's: nothing added, nothing trimmed, even when the audience hates it.

The verb in verse 8, 'seized,' is a general word for grasping or laying hold of, and Jeremiah 2:8 uses its participle of the priests who 'handle' the law without knowing the LORD. The people who laid hands on the law now lay hands on its messenger.

The Hebrew word for 'disaster' in verse 3 is the same root as 'evil' in 'the evil of their deeds.' The text makes the link deliberately: the ra'ah God plans is a response to the ra' the people have done, and the call to 'turn, each from his evil way,' is meant to remove the ground for it. Verse 6 adds a word for 'cursing,' qelalah, so the city that should be a blessing among the nations would become their byword for ruin, the very reversal of what Abraham's line was meant to be, Genesis 12:3.

Verse 17 names the 'elders of the land,' a standing body of judges and advisers, and verse 10 the 'officials,' the royal court. The text distinguishes the two groups because it is the combination, popular memory plus royal authority, that blocks the mob.

Finally, Jeremiah's phrase in verse 14, 'do to me what you think is good and right,' hands the case over to those who would judge. Its force is that the one who says it already knows what is good and right, and cannot be cowed: the content of what is good and right has just been set out in verse 13.

typology.type: Jeremiah on trial for threatening the temple
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah is seized in the temple courts and charged with a capital offence for foretelling the temple's fall, Jeremiah 26:8 to 9. Jesus is tried by the Sanhedrin on a charge built from a saying about destroying the temple, Matthew 26:61 and Mark 14:58, and Stephen is accused of the same, Acts 6:13 to 14. The escalation is that Jesus' words were true in a way His accusers did not grasp, John 2:19 to 21, and that He did not escape. The type falls short because Jeremiah was spared by a protector and by precedent, while Christ went through the verdict to the cross.

Jeremiah warns that killing him will bring 'innocent blood' on the city, Jeremiah 26:15. The idea is that the blood of the righteous cries out against those who shed it, as Abel's did, Genesis 4:10. Jesus names this long line of murdered messengers, Matthew 23:35, and the crowd at His trial accepts the guilt in Matthew 27:25, while Pilate washes his hands in Matthew 27:24. The escalation is that the blood of Christ, unlike Abel's, 'speaks a better word,' Hebrews 12:24, since it speaks forgiveness rather than only accusation. The type falls short because Jeremiah's blood could only accuse.

typology.type: Uriah, the faithful prophet who is killed
typology.fulfillment: Uriah says the same things as Jeremiah, flees, and is dragged back from Egypt to die by the sword, Jeremiah 26:20 to 23. He is the pattern of the prophets who died for the word, Hebrews 11:37, and of the Son sent last, Matthew 21:35 to 39. The correspondence is that his death exposes the real attitude of the rulers to God's message. The escalation is that Christ's death was not the failure of a mission but its means, Hebrews 9:26. The type falls short in that Uriah's death accomplished nothing for others.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ first by identity of charge. Jesus is condemned for a saying about the temple, and what Jeremiah said in the courtyard, that God's house could become Shiloh, Jesus said at the end of His ministry: 'Not one stone here will be left on another,' a verdict that fell in AD 70. In cleansing the temple He quoted Jeremiah 7:11, 'a den of robbers,' Matthew 21:13, tying His action to the very sermon that is on trial here. Like Jeremiah, He was handed over by the priests, and, like Jeremiah's accusers, they thought they were defending God's house.

It leads to Christ by the ruling that the elders reach for in verse 19. They plead precedent, and the precedent is mercy: Hezekiah 'feared the LORD and sought His favor.' Jesus is the one who offers the final form of that mercy. The warning that Jeremiah delivered, that Jerusalem's persistence would make it a ruin, is the one Jesus delivered in tears, Luke 19:41 to 44, and the longing in Luke 13:34, 'how often I have longed to gather your children together,' is the same call to turn that Jeremiah makes in verse 13.

It leads to Christ by contrast. Jeremiah is rescued by Ahikam's hand. Jesus, who had the right to call on legions of angels, Matthew 26:53, does not call for rescue. The very ruling that spared Jeremiah, that a prophet speaking in the LORD's name is not worthy of death, verse 16, is the verdict the Sanhedrin refused to reach, though Pilate's wife and Pilate himself proclaim Jesus innocent, Matthew 27:19 and 27:24. And where Uriah's death only exposed a guilty king, the death of Christ bore the guilt, 1 Peter 2:24.

It leads to Christ by the 'innocent blood.' Jeremiah told Judah what it would mean to kill him. The cross shows the ultimate case: the blood of the only wholly innocent One is poured out, and instead of the curse that Jeremiah feared for the city, it becomes the blood of the new covenant, Luke 22:20, the promise at the heart of the next chapters of this book.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Jeremiah is not Christ, and Uriah is not a veiled picture of Him. Their stories belong to a long line of prophets whom the New Testament holds together, and Jesus, the final Prophet, enters that line and completes it.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who sends warnings before He sends judgment, and who builds mercy into the warning. 'Perhaps they will listen and turn,' verse 3, is a remarkable thing for the Lord of all to say, and the word 'again and again' in verse 5, which echoes His sending of the prophets through the whole history, shows that the delay of judgment is not weakness but patience. His relenting is a promise as well as a threat: He is willing to change course for any people who turn, verse 13, and He did so for Hezekiah's generation, verse 19.

He is a God who values the word spoken in His name. 'Do not omit a word,' verse 2, treats His message as something that must not be trimmed to suit the audience. And He holds the line on innocent blood, verse 15. He is not indifferent to what is done to His servants, and the city that shed it would answer for it.

The chapter also holds a tension that readers should not smooth over: God saves Jeremiah and permits Uriah to die. The text gives no explanation. It credits Jeremiah's survival to an ordinary human act, Ahikam's support, in verse 24, and it records Uriah's death without comment. What it will not allow is that God has lost control. Elsewhere in this very book the LORD says that He knew Jeremiah before he was formed, Jeremiah 1:5, and that He would rescue him, Jeremiah 1:19. The God who protects here does not promise protection from every death, and the Bible's answer to that is the cross and the resurrection, not an explanation.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to honour a God who tells hard truths and to pray for the courage to say them. It also teaches us to trust Him with the outcome. The prophet's calm in verse 14, 'here I am in your hands,' is possible only for someone who knows that he is first in the hands of God.

crossReferences.note: The temple sermon itself, with its famous 'the temple of the LORD' chant and its call to look at Shiloh. Chapter 26 is the sequel: it tells what the sermon cost. Read together they show both the content of the warning and the reaction it provoked.

The prophecy the elders quote in 26:18. Its setting is a corrupt leadership that still says 'No disaster can come upon us.' The match with Jerusalem's confidence in Jeremiah's day is exact, and the quotation shows that the book of Micah was known and respected a century on.

Records that God 'abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh.' It confirms that Jeremiah's Shiloh warning rests on what the people already sang: a holy place is not a guarantee, and God can leave a shrine that His people profane.

States the principle behind the elders' argument and Jeremiah's appeal. Announced disaster is withdrawn when a nation turns. It shows that 26:3, 26:13 and 26:19 are an application of a rule God had already given the prophet.

Jehoiakim again, this time burning the scroll with a penknife. Elnathan, who fetched Uriah in 26:22, is among those who plead with the king here. It shows the same king, the same court and the same pressure on Jeremiah, a few years later.

The law of the false prophet that the priests and prophets invoke in 26:11. It gives them real grounds for a trial and shows the danger of applying a rule to a true prophet. The test the law supplies is the one the elders' memory of Micah in effect applies.

The Sanhedrin seeks testimony against Jesus and finally settles on a saying about destroying the temple. The charge is the same one raised against Jeremiah, and the setting, priests seeking a prophet's death, is much the same.

Jesus says a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem and mourns the city that kills the prophets. He places Himself in the line of Jeremiah and Uriah and shows that the story of 26:20 to 23 was not an isolated case.
Stephen asks which prophet the fathers did not persecute. His question is the long view of what chapter 26 shows in miniature, and it points to the climax in the killing of the Righteous One.

Lists the faithful who were put to death by the sword. Uriah, killed by Jehoiakim's sword in Jeremiah 26:23, belongs among them, and the verse reminds readers that faith is sometimes honoured by rescue and sometimes by endurance.

study.oneStory:
The question under this chapter is old: what does God do with a people who trust His house more than Him? At the beginning, Eden was the first sanctuary and exile from it the first consequence of distrust, Genesis 3:23 to 24. Israel's temple, in the same story, was a place where God chose to dwell among sinners, and the whole system of sacrifice, priesthood and holy space was a mercy, not a possession. Jeremiah 26 is the moment when the guardians of that mercy treat it as a guarantee, and the prophet who says otherwise is nearly killed.

The chapter stands in the middle of a long pattern. A prophet speaks, the leaders resist, a remnant remembers. Micah in Hezekiah's day, Jeremiah in Jehoiakim's, and later Stephen and the apostles all play the part of the messenger the leaders cannot silence and cannot hear. Behind each is the God who sends again and again, Jeremiah 26:5, and the verse turns into a summary of the whole Old Testament: God keeps sending, and the people keep refusing.

It also sets up what follows. The same book that records a threat of death for speaking of the temple's fall goes on to record the temple's fall, in 586 BC, and then, in chapters 30 and 31, the promise of a new covenant. The judgment Jeremiah spoke about is real, and it is not the last word. The one who is finally condemned for speaking about the temple, Jesus, is the one who raises the true temple in three days, John 2:19 to 21, and builds a people who are themselves the dwelling of God, Ephesians 2:21 to 22.

In the new creation the question is answered for good. John sees no temple in the city, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The place that could be trusted falsely is replaced by the Presence that can be trusted truly, and the prophets who were killed for speaking of it are vindicated, Revelation 11:18.

quiz.q: What specific message provokes the crowd to seize Jeremiah and demand his death?

options.text: That the LORD's house could become like Shiloh, a ruin, and Jerusalem an object of cursing, if the people did not turn.
options.note: Verses 6 and 9 show this exact warning about the temple's fate as the trigger for the mob's fury.

options.text: That Babylon would soon be destroyed by Judah's armies.
options.note: Jeremiah's message is a warning against Judah and its temple, not a prediction of Babylon's defeat.

options.text: That Jeremiah himself should be made king.
options.note: There is no claim to kingship in this passage; the offense is the prophecy against the temple and city.

options.text: That the priests should raise the temple taxes.
options.note: The offense concerns a prophecy of judgment on the temple and city, not a financial matter.

quiz.q: What precedent do the elders cite to argue for sparing Jeremiah's life?

options.text: That Micah prophesied an almost identical judgment in Hezekiah's day and was not put to death, and the LORD relented because Hezekiah sought His favor.
options.note: Verses 18 to 19 recall Micah's prophecy and its outcome as direct historical precedent.

options.text: That Jeremiah was a member of the royal family and so exempt from punishment.
options.note: The elders' argument rests on prophetic and historical precedent, not royal status.

options.text: That the law required a trial to last at least one year before execution.
options.note: No such legal technicality is cited; the argument is about the precedent of Micah and Hezekiah's response.

options.text: That Jeremiah had already left the country and could not be tried.
options.note: Jeremiah is present and defends himself directly before the officials in this chapter.

quiz.q: What happens to the prophet Uriah, who preached the same message as Jeremiah?

options.text: He fled to Egypt in fear, was brought back by King Jehoiakim's men, and was executed.
options.note: Verses 20 to 23 record his flight, forced return, and death by the sword.

options.text: He was honored by King Jehoiakim for his courage.
options.note: Jehoiakim actively sought Uriah's death and had him executed upon capture.

options.text: He successfully escaped and was never found.
options.note: The text records that he was found in Egypt and brought back to Judah.

options.text: He recanted his prophecy and was pardoned.
options.note: There is no record of recantation; he was executed despite fleeing.

quiz.q: Who ultimately protects Jeremiah from being handed over to the people for execution?

options.text: Ahikam son of Shaphan.
options.note: Verse 24 names Ahikam specifically as Jeremiah's protector.

options.text: King Jehoiakim himself.
options.note: Jehoiakim is shown seeking Uriah's death in this same chapter, not protecting Jeremiah.

options.text: The priests and prophets who first seized him.
options.note: The priests and prophets are the ones demanding his death, not protecting him.

options.text: Micah the Moreshite, appearing personally in the narrative.
options.note: Micah's prophecy is cited as precedent from the past; he does not appear as a character in this scene.

quiz.q: How does this chapter anticipate Christ's own trial in the Gospels?

options.text: Jesus faces the identical charge, threatening to destroy the temple, before the same kind of hostile religious authorities.
options.note: Matthew 26:61 records the exact same accusation later brought against Jesus at His trial.

options.text: There is no meaningful parallel between this chapter and Christ's trial.
options.note: The charge concerning the temple is a direct, specific parallel between the two trials.

options.text: Jesus was accused of a completely different crime with no relation to the temple.
options.note: The Gospel accounts specifically record the temple-related charge as central to Jesus' trial.

options.text: The parallel is only that both trials took place in Jerusalem.
options.note: The connection is specifically the shared charge concerning the temple, not merely the shared location.

questions: Jeremiah was told to 'not omit a word', even the hardest parts of God's message. Is there a hard truth you have been softening or leaving out when you should speak it fully?
The elders remembered Micah's precedent and it saved Jeremiah's life. Where might remembering how God has worked faithfully in the past help you face a hard situation now?
Uriah fled in fear rather than trusting God with the outcome of his faithfulness. Where are you tempted to run from a cost of obedience rather than trusting God with the result?
God's warning of disaster was always conditioned on whether people would turn. Is there a warning in your own life right now that is meant to lead you to repentance rather than despair?

Jeremiah faced the same charge Jesus later faced, and Ahikam's protection saved him where nothing saved Uriah. How does knowing Christ ultimately was not spared change how you think about the cost of faithfulness?

translationNotes.note: 'Like Shiloh' refers to the earlier sanctuary site destroyed after Israel's unfaithfulness, 1 Samuel 4, a well-known historical warning that God's presence does not guarantee a place's permanent protection regardless of the people's conduct.

This is one of the only places in the Old Testament where one prophetic book directly quotes another by name and cites its historical outcome, Micah 3:12, confirming both the accuracy of the earlier prophecy and its function as legal precedent.

Ahikam son of Shaphan belonged to an influential family that supported Josiah's reforms and later Jeremiah's ministry; his son Gedaliah would later be appointed governor of Judah after Jerusalem's fall, chapter 40.
